arguments.literal: Authority is an identity-bearing semantic relation, not a display label, capability string, actor identity or reachable code path. Its identity preserves owner, kind, governed subject, scope and governing basis.
IDENTITY §6 (STDO-UP-004); P6, P3; the Authority object and its kinds are FOUNDATIONS §2
Authority is never minted from capability, a label or reachability.

Composition, delegation, adapters, projections, wrappers and registries may restrict or faithfully carry admitted authority. They do not silently widen scope, add a role, increase cardinality, change kind, or reconstruct authority from actor identity, payload shape or available capability. Elevation, transfer, split, merge, proxy grant, revocation and retirement each require an explicit authority decision and an identifiable basis.
IDENTITY §6 (STDO-UP-004); P6, P4b

The substrate or runtime may define default identities for runtime-owned objects, such as runs, function calls, jobs, execution frames, continuations and events. For these, the engine may use opaque identities and engine-local generation rules. Those rules should optimise for uniqueness, replay safety and event-stream integrity. The engine should not impose domain-specific semantic grammar on domain-owned objects. Derived domains own the semantic identity grammar for their own constitutional objects, such as requirements, requirement families, acceptance criteria, scenarios, ADRs or design decisions, and published domain assets. The domain defines which identity kinds exist, how they are distinguished, what makes them unique, and how they are parsed or read. The runtime may transport those identities, but it should not silently invent their meaning.
IDENTITY §5 Authority split; P3, P6

Identity should remain stable for the governed lifecycle it serves. This does not mean every identity is immutable forever. It means identity is stable enough to support traceability, comparison, replay, publication and supersession. If an identity changes, the method should make the relationship explicit rather than silently reusing the old identity for a different object.
IDENTITY §2 Stability; P3, P4b

Identity is always scoped. At minimum, identity should be interpretable through authority, kind and value. So the minimum semantic model is: identity = authority + kind + value. This is the scoped identity of an Object (FOUNDATIONS §2). Optional additional coordinates may include parent scope, revision, publication version and temporal coordinates.
IDENTITY §2 Scoped identity; P3; the Object is FOUNDATIONS §2

Identity is unique within its lawful scope. The requirement is not that every identity looks globally unique as a naked string. The requirement is: no two live objects of the same kind may share the same identity within the same authority scope; aliasing across scopes remains explicit; and serialisation preserves enough hierarchy to prevent accidental collision.
IDENTITY §2 Uniqueness; P3

Identity is typed. Different kinds of thing should not be collapsed into one undifferentiated identity space. Examples of distinct identity kinds include goal, intent, requirement, requirement_family, acceptance_criterion, scenario, design_decision, published_function, carrier_surface, release, install, run, function_call, continuation and event. The method does not treat a family identity as if it were a concrete requirement identity, or a release version as if it were object identity.
IDENTITY §2 Type; P3
An object's scoped identity (authority, kind, value) survives admissible state change and encoding change.

Human authority may act directly or through an explicitly admitted bounded proxy. Proxy actor identity and human-authority identity remain distinct; a profile's own surfaces may project the human-authority relation under that profile's term. A proxy grant names its grantor, actor, subject, scope, permitted and excluded decisions, validity, delegation rights, revocation and provenance.
IDENTITY §6 (STDO-UP-004); P6, P3

A direct or proxied decision preserves its source, subject and basis, acting identity and mode, scope, change class, disposition and supersession. Recording a ruling cannot widen it. Proxy authority does not make implementer self-review independent and does not confer unrelated runtime or domain authority.
IDENTITY §6 (STDO-UP-004); P6, P4b; EVALUATION §5 applies this law to acceptance

symbols.label: Actor identity: the human, agent, tool or process performing the work; an identity, not an authority

Authority: an identity-bearing permission to operate or to dispose acceptance within a scope; never minted from capability, label or reachability; its kinds are frame-set, semantic, evaluation, operation and decision authority
Object O: a subject with scoped identity (authority, kind, value), boundary, current state and declared material relations
Proxy: an explicitly admitted bounded relation through which a human decision is exercised
Scoped identity: identity = authority + kind + value, the scoped identity of an Object; optional coordinates add parent scope, revision, publication version and time
Authority identity: authority as an identity-bearing semantic relation preserving owner, kind, governed subject, scope and governing basis

Domain-owned identity: the semantic identity grammar a derived domain owns for its constitutional objects such as requirements, acceptance criteria, scenarios, design decisions and published domain assets
Engine-owned identity: a default, possibly opaque identity the substrate or runtime defines for runtime-owned objects such as runs, function calls, jobs, frames, continuations and events
Identity kind: the type of an identity (goal, requirement, requirement_family, release, run, event and so on); different kinds should not be collapsed into one identity space
Proxy grant: the record by which human authority admits a bounded proxy; names grantor, actor, subject, scope, permitted and excluded decisions, validity, delegation rights, revocation and provenance
Recorded decision: a direct or proxied authority decision with its source, subject, basis, acting identity and mode, scope, change class, disposition and supersession
